lead: An on-off controller has only two outputs: full on and full off. It compares output y with reference r, takes error e = r − y, and switches when e crosses a threshold. The output cannot settle at the set point; it overshoots, switches and cycles. This limit cycle is normal. Thermostats, fridge compressors, water-level pumps and irons use it because their actuator is a relay, contactor or valve. Only a few universities teach this in detail.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 closed-loop block diagrams and Unit 2 first-order response.

blocks.text: Write e = r − y. r is set point, y is output, e is error. An ideal two-position controller gives u = U<sub>max</sub> when e > 0 and u = U<sub>min</sub> when e < 0. u is controller output; U<sub>max</sub> is the upper level (heater on); U<sub>min</sub> is the lower level (heater off). At e = 0 the output is held or undefined.

A real relay has hysteresis ±h. It switches on only when e > +h and off only when e < −h. h is in the units of the error, i.e. of the measured variable, e.g. °C. Full dead band is 2h. Hysteresis stops chatter from noise; a wider band gives fewer switches but a larger swing. The controller remembers its last state inside the band, so it is not a pure function of e.
u = U<sub>max</sub> if e > +h; u = U<sub>min</sub> if e < −h
blocks.where: e = r − y is error; h is half the hysteresis band; U<sub>max</sub> and U<sub>min</sub> are the two output levels.

blocks.text: For a first-order plant, let a be rise rate and b fall rate near the set point. a and b are rise and fall rates in units of the measured variable per minute, e.g. °C/min. The output travels 2h. On time t<sub>on</sub> = 2h/a. Off time t<sub>off</sub> = 2h/b. Cycle T = t<sub>on</sub> + t<sub>off</sub>. Duty D = t<sub>on</sub>/T.

blocks.where: t<sub>on</sub> is on time; t<sub>off</sub> is off time; D is duty cycle in percent.

blocks.text: A tank heater with a = 0.5 °C/min, b = 0.2 °C/min and h = 1 °C gives t<sub>on</sub> = 4 min, t<sub>off</sub> = 10 min, T = 14 min, D = 28.6 %. Average power D×U<sub>max</sub> + (1−D)×U<sub>min</sub> is only an energy balance, not a linear gain.
A second-order plant can ring. Its limit cycle is built from linear response pieces between switches; amplitude and period depend on damping and h.

sections.h3: Relay model and where it is used

blocks.text: Model the ideal relay as u = U<sub>avg</sub> + (U<sub>max</sub>−U<sub>min</sub>)/2 × sign(e), where U<sub>avg</sub> = (U<sub>max</sub>+U<sub>min</sub>)/2. With U<sub>min</sub> = 0, U<sub>avg</sub> = U<sub>max</sub>/2. The output jumps between two fixed levels at e = 0, so there is no finite slope (no gain) there; the output is bounded between U<sub>min</sub> and U<sub>max</sub>. The relay is nonlinear, so one transfer function cannot describe the whole loop.

Use on-off control with a contactor, solenoid valve, relay or thyristor switch. It is cheap and robust, but poor when cycling wears valves or tight control is needed. PWM makes the average continuous; PID is the next step (see 5.2). Relay auto-tuning uses the same limit cycle to estimate ultimate gain and period. Some syllabi call this two-position control.

figure.caption: The tank temperature rises from 60 °C to 62 °C in 4 min and cools back in 10 min. The 14 min cycle is set by the hysteresis band and the two rates.

spec.aria: A sawtooth plot of tank temperature rising from 60 to 62 degrees Celsius in 4 minutes and cooling back in 10 minutes, repeating.

examples.question: A tank heater switches on at 60 °C and off at 62 °C. With the heater on the temperature rises at 0.5 °C/min; with the heater off it falls at 0.2 °C/min. Find the on time, off time, cycle time and duty cycle.
examples.answer: On time = 4 min, off time = 10 min, cycle time = 14 min, duty cycle = 28.6 %.
examples.check:
rise=0.5
fall=0.2
band=2.0
on=band/rise
off=band/fall
cycle=on+off
duty=round(on/cycle*100,1)
print(f"{on:.1f}")
print(f"{off:.1f}")
print(f"{cycle:.1f}")
print(f"{duty:.1f}")

traps: Ignoring hysteresis gives infinite switching; a real loop has a limit cycle, and average output is not a linear gain.
Sign: e = r − y; e > 0 means y is below set point, so a heater switches on. Swapping the sign reverses the action.
Hysteresis width is 2h, not h. Using h halves the calculated on and off times.
Duty cycle is t_on/T, not the ratio Umax/Umin.
On-off has no proportional gain; do not use a fixed K for stability checks.

quiz.q: State the ideal on-off law with e = r − y.
quiz.a: u = Umax if e > 0; u = Umin if e < 0.
The dead band blocks noise toggles, so fewer switches occur.

quiz.q: Set point 50 °C, hysteresis ±0.5 °C, rise 0.25 °C/min, fall 0.1 °C/min. Find t_on, t_off and T.
quiz.a: Band = 1 °C; t_on = 4 min; t_off = 10 min; T = 14 min.

quiz.q: A heater is on 3 min and off 12 min. Find duty cycle.
Double the hysteresis band with the same rates. What happens to period and duty?
quiz.a: On and off times double; period doubles; duty stays the same.

quiz.q: Why can an on-off controller not hold a steady output at the set point?
quiz.a: It has only two outputs, so it always overshoots and cycles.

quiz.q: A tank cools faster for the same band. What happens to duty cycle?
quiz.a: Off time becomes shorter; on time is unchanged, so duty rises.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, on-off control appears in PLCs and thermostats, often refined as time-proportioning or PWM so the average power is smooth. Relay feedback is also the basis of auto-tuning: a deliberately injected limit cycle estimates ultimate gain and period. Search terms: two-position control, relay auto-tuning, time-proportioning control, and chatter in relay loops.
